judicial-examinations.metaTitle: Judicial examinations — types under the classifier
judicial-examinations.metaDescription: Trace, ballistic, explosives, phototechnical and portrait, soil and biological examinations under codes 05–08 and 11 of the classifier: types, objects, and research tasks.
intro: This direction brings together the classical forensic examinations under codes 05, 06, 07, 08, and 11 of the national classifier of judicial examination types. They are carried out within court proceedings and extrajudicially — at the request of individuals, advocates, and organizations.

The subjects of research are items of physical evidence: traces, weapons and ammunition, photographic materials, and objects of soil, plant, and animal origin. The study ends with a substantiated conclusion that can be presented in court.

items.title: Technical condition examination of a residential building
items.summary: A court-appointed technical condition examination of a nine-storey residential building where the residents had reported progressing cracks in load-bearing walls and moisture in the basement.
items.task: The court needed an independent assessment of the building's technical condition: whether the reported defects threaten structural safety, what caused them, and what repair works are required.
work: Review of the building's design and as-built documentation
Visual and instrumental inspection of load-bearing structures, facades and common areas
Measurement of crack widths and deformation markers with follow-up monitoring
Analysis of the foundation condition and the basement moisture regime
Comparison of the revealed defects with the normative requirements for safe operation
items.result: The conclusion described the building's actual technical condition, classified the defects by cause and severity, and formulated a list of necessary repair works. The report was accepted by the court as the basis for obliging the management company to carry out the repairs.

items.title: Circumstances and damage study after a road accident
items.summary: An auto-technical examination after a collision between a passenger car and a delivery van at a city intersection, appointed within a civil dispute over compensation.
items.task: Determine the mechanism of the collision, the speed and trajectories of the vehicles before the impact, and whether the drivers' actions complied with the traffic rules; separately assess the extent of damage to the car.
work: Study of the case materials, the accident scene schematic and the vehicle documents
Analysis of the vehicles' kinematics before and at the moment of the collision
Assessment of the technical condition of the brakes, steering and lights of both vehicles
Verification of the damage extent against the submitted repair estimate
items.result: The examination established the collision mechanism and the traffic signal mode at the moment of the accident, which allowed the court to distribute liability between the parties. The damage calculation was corrected: part of the claimed works was not related to the accident.

items.title: Real estate valuation of a shopping center
items.summary: A market valuation of a shopping center building with an adjacent land plot, prepared at a bank's request for a collateral transaction.
items.task: Determine the market value of the property as of the valuation date, analyzing its income potential, technical condition and the state of the commercial real estate market.
work: Inspection and description of the building and the land plot
Analysis of the lease agreements and the center's actual income
Study of the commercial real estate market and comparable transactions
Value calculation by the income, comparative and cost approaches with reconciliation of the results
items.result: The report determined the market and liquidation value of the property with a full justification of the applied approaches. The valuation was accepted by the bank for the collateral transaction.

items.title: Land plot boundary surveying and cadastral works
items.imageLabel: Surveying works at a construction site
items.summary: Boundary surveying and cadastral works on a disputed land plot in the Kotayk region, where according to the cadastre the neighboring plot boundaries overlapped.
items.task: Restore the actual boundaries of the plot on the ground, compare them with the cadastral records, and establish the causes of the boundary overlap with the neighboring plots.
work: Analysis of the title documents and cadastral maps of the plot and the neighboring plots
Field surveying with an electronic total station and GNSS equipment
Comparison of the measured boundaries with the coordinates recorded in the cadastre
Preparation of a boundary plan and a conclusion on the causes of the discrepancy
items.result: The works established the actual position of the boundaries and quantified the deviation from the cadastral data. The boundary plan allowed the parties to correct the records and resolve the dispute without further litigation.

items.title: Composite examination in a property ownership dispute
items.summary: A composite judicial examination appointed in a dispute over the ownership of a commercial property: the contested transaction documents required both document research and a valuation of the property.
items.task: Verify the authenticity and the time of execution of the signatures on the sale agreement and its copies, and determine the market value of the property for the period stated in the disputed documents.
work: Document research of the agreement: paper, printing features, signatures and entries
Comparison of the handwriting samples with the parties' signature specimens
Technical examination of the copies for signs of partial replacement of the text
Market valuation of the property for the period stated in the documents
items.result: The research revealed signs of a later addition in one of the copies and established the value of the property for the required period. The composite conclusion gave the court a single evidentiary basis for the decision.

items.title: Construction defects examination in a new residential complex
items.imageLabel: Wall with cracks and peeling paint
items.summary: An examination of the quality of construction and finishing works in a newly commissioned residential complex, initiated by a buyer who refused to accept the apartment.
items.task: Verify whether the revealed defects — cracks in partition walls, uneven floor screeds and poor window installation — are construction defects, and determine the scope and cost of their elimination.
work: Review of the construction documentation and the acceptance certificate
Instrumental inspection of the apartment: walls, floors, window openings and utility systems
Identification and classification of the defects with photo fixation
Calculation of the scope and cost of the remedial works
items.result: The conclusion confirmed the presence of defects attributable to the developer and calculated the cost of their elimination. The parties settled the dispute, and the developer eliminated the defects at his own expense.

items.title: Market valuation of apartments in a civil dispute
items.summary: A valuation of two apartments in the center of Yerevan, appointed by a court in an inheritance division dispute between co-owners.
items.task: Determine the market value of each apartment as of a single date so that the court could divide the estate equitably between the parties.
work: Inspection and description of both apartments and verification of their legal status
Analysis of the residential property market segment in the respective districts
Selection of comparable transactions and adjustment for the differences
Final value determination by the comparative approach with a sensitivity check
items.result: The report provided a justified market value for each property. The court used the valuation to determine the compensation due to the party who did not receive a share of the property.

items.title: Damage assessment after a fire in commercial premises
items.summary: An assessment of the damage caused by a fire in premises rented by a retail company, prepared for an insurance claim and a dispute with the lessor.
items.task: Determine the extent of the damage to the premises, the finishing, the equipment and the goods, and calculate the total amount of losses caused by the fire and the firefighting operations.
work: Inspection of the premises and photo fixation of the damage
Analysis of the documents on the property, the equipment and the stock
Assessment of the repair works needed to restore the premises
Calculation of the total losses with a breakdown by category
items.result: The report calculated the full amount of the losses, separating the fire damage from the consequential damage caused by firefighting water. The calculated figures were used in the insurance settlement.

items.title: What is a judicial examination and when do you need one
items.excerpt: A judicial examination is one of the main sources of evidence in a case. We explain when a court orders one and what questions are put to the expert.
body: A judicial examination is a study ordered by the court to establish the facts of a case on a scientific basis. When resolving a dispute requires specialised knowledge — in construction, valuation, accounting, or engineering — the court refers the matter to a qualified expert.

The questions put to the expert are formulated by the parties and approved by the court. They may concern the causes of damage, the quality of works, the value of property, or the reliability of documents. How precisely the questions are worded determines the practical value of the conclusion.

The conclusion is assessed by the court within the general system of evidence, together with the other materials of the case. That is why it is essential that the research is carried out independently, transparently, and with sound methodology.

items.title: Property valuation: what documents you need
items.excerpt: The accuracy and turnaround of a valuation largely depend on a complete document set. We list the package required for real estate and vehicles.
body: A real estate valuation usually requires the ownership document, the cadastral passport, and the owner's identification. If the valuation is prepared for lending or for a court case, additional documents related to the matter may also be needed.
For vehicles the basis is the registration certificate and the technical passport; in accident cases, also photographs of the damage and the service invoices.
A complete package shortens the valuation period and rules out repeated visits. If a document is missing, the expert will help identify how to obtain it before the work begins.

items.title: Auto-technical examination after an accident: step by step
items.excerpt: From the first actions at the scene to the final conclusion — a short guide that protects your rights.
body: Right after an accident, record the scene: photograph the location, the position of the vehicles, and the visible damage. These become the baseline material for the later examination.
An auto-technical examination answers the questions that cannot be resolved by eye: the mechanism of the crash, whether the damage matches it, and the scope and cost of repairs.
The conclusion can support an insurance claim, pre-trial negotiations, or a lawsuit. The more precise the research, the stronger your position.

items.title: Reading an expert conclusion in court
items.excerpt: The structure of a conclusion — from introduction to findings — and which sections matter most for the outcome of the case.
body: Every conclusion has three parts: introductory (who ordered the research and on what basis), analytical (which methods and results), and final (the expert's answers to the questions posed).

When reading, note that under each answer the expert cites the method and the sources. Cases where a question went unanswered or received a qualified answer are stated as well — they may ground additional questions.
The parties may ask the court to have the conclusion clarified or to order a repeat examination if there are serious grounds to doubt its methodology.

items.title: Construction-technical expertise in construction disputes
items.excerpt: From quality requirements to the causes of defects — why a construction dispute is decided by an on-site investigation.
body: Construction disputes usually arise over the scope, quality, or timing of works. Documents alone rarely resolve them: an on-site inspection, measurements, and an assessment of materials are needed.
A construction-technical examination answers whether the completed works match the design and the standards, what the defects are, what caused them, and what their remediation will cost.
Such a conclusion lets the parties move a contested issue from emotions into the field of facts — measurable indicators.

items.title: Damage assessment after an incident: steps and documents
items.excerpt: In case of water, fire, or property damage — how to document the loss so it is accepted in an insurance or court proceeding.
body: A damage assessment starts with recording the circumstances: photographs, witness details, service reports and invoices. These documents tie the damage to a specific incident.
The expert calculates the actual restoration cost, taking depreciation and local market prices into account, and formulates a conclusion that can be submitted to the insurer or the court.
Timing matters: the sooner the state of things is recorded, the less room there is to dispute the valuation.

items.title: Accounting expertise in economic disputes
items.excerpt: Financial figures often decide the outcome of a case. When is an accounting examination needed and what can it show?
body: Economic disputes — debt, shareholder, contractual — often come down to the same question: what does the accounting actually show? That is exactly where an accounting examination comes in.
The expert reconstructs the accounting picture from primary documents, verifies the correctness of the calculations, and provides answers about the monetary figures in the conclusion.
Such research also helps investors and managers understand the real financial position before going to court.

items.title: Real estate valuation methods: comparative, income, and cost
items.excerpt: Why the same property yields three different values under three methods — and which method fits which case.
body: The comparative method relies on recently closed deals on the market and is justified when enough similar objects exist. The income method values a property through the income it generates — for commercial and rental real estate.
The cost method calculates what an identical object would cost to build today, minus depreciation. It applies to special-purpose properties and insurance questions.
The appraiser chooses the method based on the type of the object and the purpose of the valuation, and explains the choice in the conclusion. That choice determines the final figure.

items.title: Document research: when the reliability of a signature matters
items.excerpt: A technical examination of a seal, signature, or text can decide a dispute over an inheritance, a contract, or a debt.
body: When a contested document appears in a case — a will, a contract, a loan receipt — the parties usually stand by their own versions. Technical examination replaces that standoff with facts.
The examination can answer whether the signature was made by the named person, whether the text was written in one sitting, and whether the document was altered.
The findings can ground both criminal and civil proceedings, which is why the research must follow procedural requirements.

items.title: Geodetic and cadastral works: checking boundaries before a purchase
items.excerpt: The real boundaries of a plot and the cadastral data do not always match. How to avoid a dispute with the neighbours.
body: One of the main risks when buying land is a mismatch between the cadastral map and the terrain. Geodetic measurements reveal the problem before the transaction.
Cadastral works include establishing the plot on the ground, calculating its area, and, where necessary, correcting the data in the cadastral system.
Measurements made before the purchase are inexpensive insurance against boundary disputes and costly re-issuing of documents.

items.title: Your rights during a judicial examination
items.excerpt: The parties are not passive observers. What rights you have when an examination is ordered and while it is carried out.
body: At the stage of ordering the examination, the parties may propose questions to the expert, submit their documents, and ask for an expert of a particular specialisation.
During the research you may read the conclusion, request clarifications and, with convincing grounds, challenge it and ask for a repeat examination.
An active position does not mean distrust of the expert: it is a procedural mechanism that makes the case more transparent.

items.title: The legal regulation of judicial expertise: key provisions
items.excerpt: Who may act as an expert, what requirements a conclusion must meet, and what the expert's responsibility means.
body: Judicial examinations are governed by the procedural codes and the legislation on expert activity. They define who may act as an expert and what requirements the research must meet.
A conclusion is evidence only when it was obtained lawfully and meets the formal requirements: the methodology, the initial data, the expert's details and signatures.
Even then the conclusion is not decisive in advance: the court assesses it in the course of the hearing. That balance is what keeps the quality of expert work high.

mission: ANIKOM LLC was founded on 30 October 2000 as a center for research and judicial examinations. The center carries out judicial and extrajudicial examinations, property valuation, geodetic and cadastral works, and damage assessment.

Our mission is to deliver objective, independent, and evidence-based conclusions that courts, public bodies, companies, and individuals can rely on. We work so that every conclusion stands up to professional and legal scrutiny.
